claim: Fibronectin is abundant in the interstitial space of multicellular spheroids made of CT26 cells.
source: The presence of hydrated extracellular matrix is evidenced by the abundance of fibronectin in the interstitial space (Figure 1a and Appendix 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining shown in Figure 1a and referenced in the text.

claim: The extracellular matrix is 100- to 1000-fold more compressible than cells.
source: As the ECM is 100- to 1000-fold more compressible than the cells, it absorbs most of the deformation, but still transmits the mechanical stress to the cells.
evidence: This is stated as a known property in the manuscript and is used to support the hypothesis.

claim: An osmotic pressure of a few kPa strongly reduces cell proliferation within multicellular aggregates but has no effect on individual cells cultured on a Petri dish in the absence of ECM.
source: Second, whereas an osmotic pressure of a few kPa strongly reduces the cell proliferation within multicellular aggregates, an identical pressure has no effect on individual cells cultured on a Petri dish, in the absence of ECM (Montel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Montel et al., 2011.

claim: Drugs affecting cytoskeleton organization have a negligible effect on the effective compressibility of multicellular aggregates.
source: In addition, the use of drugs affecting the cytoskeleton organization has a negligible effect on the effective compressibility of multicellular aggregates (Appendix 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data referenced in Appendix 12.

claim: Volume loss under compression in multicellular aggregates is mainly due to ECM dehydration.
source: This indicates that the volume loss under compression is mainly due to ECM dehydration (Dolega et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dolega et al., 2021.

claim: Big osmolytes do not penetrate through the ECM and induce a global compression.
source: When big enough, the osmolytes do not infiltrate the ECM and thus compress the whole aggregate by dehydrating the ECM, which in turn mechanically compresses the cells (Monnier et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Monnier et al., 2016 and is part of the experimental method description.

claim: Small osmolytes percolate through the ECM meshwork and compress the cells which can then pull on the ECM.
source: When smaller than the exclusion size of the ECM, the osmolytes percolate through the ECM meshwork and compress the cells which can then pull on the ECM (see schematic in Figure 1b–d and Appendix 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by the schematic in Figure 1b-d and Appendix 7.

claim: Fluorescent dextran molecules with a gyration radius below 5 nm equally color matrigel beads and the surrounding solution.
source: As shown in Figure 2a (top panel), fluorescent dextran molecules with a gyration radius below 5 nm (MW <70 kDa, hereafter called 'Small'; Granath, 1958) equally color the MG beads and the surrounding solution (left).
evidence: The claim is supported by the image in Figure 2a and a citation to Granath, 1958.

claim: Dextran molecules larger than 15 nm do not penetrate inside matrigel beads.
source: Conversely, dextran molecules larger than 15 nm (MW >500 kDa, Big') do not penetrate inside the MG beads, which appear darker than the surroundings (right).
evidence: The claim is supported by the image in Figure 2a showing darker beads.

claim: Big dextran molecules compress matrigel beads by 63 ± 5% at Πd=5 kPa.
source: Conversely, the same pressure caused by big dextran molecules occasions a much larger compression of 63 ± 5% (Figure 2b).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Multicellular spheroids have a typical effective osmotic modulus of Ks≃ 30 kPa, 15-folds smaller than that of individual cells.
source: Furthermore, these measurements indicate that MCS have a typical effective osmotic modulus of Ks≃ 30 kPa, 15-folds smaller than that of individual cells (Dolega et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements and a citation to Dolega et al., 2021.

claim: Small dextran molecules have no measurable effect on the volume of multicellular spheroids for moderate osmotic pressures up to Πd=10 kPa.
source: In contrast, small dextran molecules have no measurable effect on the volume of MCS, for moderate osmotic pressures (up to Πd=10 kPa).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations of MCS volume.

claim: The application of Πd with both small or big dextran leads to the same cell volume loss which does not involve the mechanical properties of the ECM but only the cell volume regulation system.
source: We show in Appendix A.5 that, for realistic estimates of the model parameters, the application of Πd with both small or big dextran leads to the same cell volume loss which does not involve the mechanical properties of the ECM but only the cell volume regulation system
evidence: The claim is derived from theoretical modeling presented in Appendix A.5.

claim: Small dextran molecules induced a ∼35 ± 10% increase in the fluorescence intensity in the interstitial space at Πd = 40 kPa.
source: In accordance with our theoretical predictions, we obtained two opposite behaviors, depending on the dextran size. Small dextran molecules induced a ∼35 ± 10% increase in the fluorescence intensity in the interstitial space (Figure 2c)
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2c (which is actually Figure 3c based on the figure caption).

claim: Big dextran caused a loss of half the fluorescence in the interstitial space, indicating that a large amount of interstitial liquid had left the intercellular space of the aggregate.
source: In contrast, for big dextran we measured a loss of half the fluorescence, meaning that a large amount of interstitial liquid had left the intercellular space of the aggregate.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements and their interpretation.

claim: Cells in control multicellular spheroids (Πd=0 Pa) present a rather uniform proliferation pattern.
source: Whereas cells in control MCS (Πd=0 Pa) present a rather uniform proliferation pattern, a global compression of MCS (big Dextran) stops cell division in the core and alters the overall MCS growth, as previously reported (Helmlinger et al., 1997; Alessandri et al., 2013; Montel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data and citations to previous work.

claim: Global compression of multicellular spheroids with big dextran stops cell division in the core and alters the overall MCS growth.
source: Whereas cells in control MCS (Πd=0 Pa) present a rather uniform proliferation pattern, a global compression of MCS (big Dextran) stops cell division in the core and alters the overall MCS growth, as previously reported (Helmlinger et al., 1997; Alessandri et al., 2013; Montel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data and citations to previous work.

claim: Under pressure, the density of Ki67-positive cells uniformly decreases across the multicellular spheroid.
source: Remarkably, under pressure the density of Ki67-positive cells uniformly decreases across the MCS.
evidence: The claim is supported by Ki67 immunostaining data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The ratio between proliferating cells in the periphery and those in the core of multicellular spheroids is 2 without pressure, 2.5 under 5 kPa exerted by small dextran, and 5 when the same pressure is exerted by big dextran.
source: Consequently, the ratio between the proliferating cells in the periphery of the MCS and those in its core increases under pressure: 2 without pressure, 2.5 under 5 kPa exerted by small dextran and 5 when the same pressure is exerted by big dextran.
evidence: The claim is derived from analysis of Ki67 staining data.

claim: The multicellular spheroid growth rate (time to double its volume) almost doubled under big dextran compression, increasing from 36 ± 1 hr for control and small dextran conditions to 68 ± 4 hr for compression with big dextran.
source: However, the MCS growth rate (time to double its volume) almost doubled under the big dextran compression, increasing from 36 ± 1 hr for the control and small dextran conditions (gray circles and blue squares, respectively) to 68 ± 4 hr for the compression with big dextran (green triangles).
evidence: The claim is supported by volumetric growth measurements shown in Figure 4c-d.

claim: Cell migration speed within multicellular spheroids was reduced by 50% at Πd = 5 kPa with big dextran compared to the unstressed case.
source: The mean migration velocity of cells was reduced by 50% at Πd = 5 kPa with big dextran, as compared to the unstressed case (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Dynamic Light Scattering measurements shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Both proliferation and motility remained almost unaltered when multicellular spheroids were exposed to Πd=5 kPa applied by small dextran.
source: Strikingly, both proliferation and motility remained almost unaltered when the MCS were exposed to an equivalent pressure (Πd=5 kPa) applied by small dextran to selectively compress the cells while leaving the native ECM unstrained (small Dextran, blue).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation and motility measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both proliferation and motility of individual cells plated in a Petri dish remained similar before and after the addition of dextran at Πd≃ 5 kPa.
source: The results (Figure 4f-g) show that both proliferation and motility remained similar, before and after the addition of dextran at a final pressure Πd≃ 5 kPa.
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4f-g.

claim: Cells grown without pressure or in the presence of small dextran were sparse in matrigel.
source: After a few days, we observed two clearly different phenotypes. Cells grown without pressure or in the presence of small dextran were sparse in the MG (Figure 5a, left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by images shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Cells cultured with big dextran proliferated locally in matrigel.
source: Conversely, cells cultured with big dextran proliferated locally (Figure 5a, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by images shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Matrigel compression appears to inhibit cell motility and to promote the formation of mini-spheroids.
source: Therefore, MG compression appears to inhibit cell motility and to promote the formation of mini-spheroids, which suggests that ECM compression has a direct effect on the cell-ECM biophysical signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from observations of cell behavior in compressed matrigel.

claim: Cells cultured in relaxed matrigel matrix show numerous protrusions and high cell anisotropy.
source: Cytoplasmic actin labeling revealed the presence of numerous protrusions, associated with high cell anisotropy, in cells cultured in a relaxed MG matrix (Figure 5b, left and middle panels)
evidence: The claim is supported by actin labeling shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Cells in compressed matrigel appeared smooth and formed round structures.
source: whereas cells appeared smooth and formed round structures, when the MG was compressed (Figure 5b, right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by actin labeling shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Cells embedded in compressed matrigel were nearly immobile.
source: Cells embedded in a compressed MG were nearly immobile, while they migrated through relaxed MG with a velocity comparable to that measured on flat surfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claim: Cells migrated through relaxed matrigel with a velocity comparable to that measured on flat surfaces.
source: Cells embedded in a compressed MG were nearly immobile, while they migrated through relaxed MG with a velocity comparable to that measured on flat surfaces.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell tracking data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claim: Cell proliferation rate drops considerably when matrigel is compressed with big dextran compared to the case without pressure and compared to the case where pressure is selectively exerted on cells with small dextran.
source: Figure 5e shows the typical time evolution of the Hoechst signal for the three conditions: proliferation rate drops considerably when the MG is compressed (Big Dextran, △), compared to the case without pressure (ο), but also compared to the case where the pressure is selectively exerted on the cells with no MG compression (Small Dextran, □).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Within the range of 2 g/l to 8 g/l, matrigel density has little to no effect on cell proliferation.
source: Our experiments show that within this range, the matrigel density has little to no effect on cell proliferation (see Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation measurements at different matrigel concentrations shown in Figure 5g.

claim: It is the compressive stress transmitted to the cells by the surrounding ECM, rather than a direct osmotic pressure on the cells, that strongly impacts cell motility and proliferation.
source: These experiments confirmed that it is the compressive stress transmitted to the cells by the surrounding ECM, rather than a direct osmotic pressure on the cells, that strongly impacts cell motility and proliferation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined results of experiments with small and big dextran.

claim: Large osmotic and mechanical pressures (of the order of 100 kPa) can cause a decrease in cell volume and consequently a deformation of the cell nucleus.
source: Large osmotic and mechanical pressures (of the order of 100 kPa) can cause a decrease in cell volume and consequently a deformation of the cell nucleus (Zhou et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2009 and Kim et al., 2015.

claim: The volume of the cell or its nucleus can be key to crucial processes such as proliferation, invasion, and differentiation.
source: It has been recently proposed that the volume of the cell or its nucleus can be key to crucial processes such as proliferation, invasion, and differentiation Guo et al., 2017; Han et al., 2020.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2017 and Han et al., 2020.

claim: Weak osmotic pressures (of the order of 1 kPa) have no measurable effect on cell volume.
source: However the weak osmotic pressures (of the order of 1 kPa) that we apply have no measurable effect on the cell volume.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations in the study.

claim: Small volume perturbations are buffered by active regulatory processes in the cell.
source: In addition, it is well-known from a biological standpoint that such small volume perturbations are buffered by active regulatory processes in the cell (Hoffmann et al., 2009; Cadart et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoffmann et al., 2009 and Cadart et al., 2019.

claim: Both cell proliferation and motility decrease in multicellular spheroids submitted to weak osmotic compression.
source: Yet, both cell proliferation and motility decrease in MCS submitted to weak osmotic compression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: For weak compressions, the cell volume is unchanged while the ECM located in between the cells is directly impacted.
source: Our results show that, for such weak compressions, the cell volume is unchanged while the ECM located in between the cells is directly impacted.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined results of the study.

claim: The mechano-sensitive role of the ECM could explain the reported evidences that osmotic pressures applied by big dextran and mechanical pressures similarly affect the growth of multicellular spheroids.
source: This mechano-sensitive role of the ECM could explain the reported evidences that osmotic pressures applied by big dextran and mechanical pressures similarly affect the growth of MCS. (Helmlinger et al., 1997; Alessandri et al., 2013; Montel et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's results and supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The reduction of the interstitial space promotes interactions between neighbouring cells, which may activate contact inhibition signals of both proliferation and locomotion.
source: First, the reduction of the interstitial space promotes interactions between neighbouring cells, which may activate contact inhibition signals of both proliferation and locomotion (Roycroft and Mayor, 2016).
evidence: The claim is a speculative mechanism supported by a citation to Roycroft and Mayor, 2016.

claim: The ECM porosity and tortuosity change within a compressed multicellular spheroid, such that its effective permeability to oxygen, nutrients, growth factors and cytokines is reduced.
source: Second, the ECM porosity and tortuosity change within a compressed MCS, such that its effective permeability to oxygen, nutrients, growth factors and cytokines is reduced and might activate inhibition signals without cell-cell contact.
evidence: The claim is a speculative mechanism based on physical reasoning.

claim: A key factor limiting the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients in multicellular spheroids is the tortuosity of the interstitial space.
source: Additionally, a key factor limiting the diffusion of oxygen and nutrients in MCS is the tortuosity of the interstitial space (Bläßle et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bläßle et al., 2018.

claim: The cell proliferation inhibition is most probably not related to hypoxia and starvation.
source: This constraint is simply absent in experiments with single cells embedded in MG, suggesting that the cell proliferation inhibition is most probably not related to hypoxia and starvation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of tortuosity effects in single cell experiments.

claim: The microscopic structure of the ECM is modified under compression (e.g. density increase and reduction of porosity), with consequences on the ECM rheology.
source: The microscopic structure of the ECM is modified under compression (e.g. density increase and reduction of porosity), with consequences on the ECM rheology.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge of ECM behavior under compression.

claim: Compression of the ECM is accompanied by an increase in its bulk modulus and a non-trivial and non-linear evolution of its stiffness.
source: Compression of the ECM is clearly accompanied by an increase in its bulk modulus and, due to its fibrillar structure, to a non-trivial and non-linear evolution of its stiffness (Sopher et al., 2018; Kurniawan et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sopher et al., 2018 and Kurniawan et al., 2016.

claim: The rheological properties of synthetic ECM have been shown to affect growth of aggregates and single cells through the regulation of stretched-activated channels.
source: For example, the rheological properties of synthetic ECM have been shown to affect growth of aggregates and single cells through the regulation of streched-activated channels (Nam et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nam et al., 2019.

claim: Integrin-dependent signals and focal adhesion assembly are regulated by the stress and strain between the cell and the ECM.
source: As integrin-dependent signals and focal adhesion assembly are regulated by the stress and strain between the cell and the ECM, the osmotic compression may steer the fate of cells in terms of morphology, migration, and differentiation (Pelham and Wang, 1997; Choquet et al., 1997; Sunyer et al., 2016; Isenberg et al., 2009; Butcher et al., 2009; Engler et al., 2006; Staunton et al., 2019; Panzetta et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The ECM is strongly modified in tumour tissues and the solid stress within tumors can reach several kPa.
source: Indeed the ECM is strongly modified in tumour tissues and the solid stress within tumors can reach several kPa, which is in accordance with the pressure applied here (Nia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nia et al., 2017.

claim: In tumors, there is a decrease in the ratio collagen/hyaluronan.
source: For example, in tumors, there is a decrease in the ratio collagen/hyaluronan (Voutouri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Voutouri et al., 2016.

claim: Hyaluronan, more hydrophilic than collagen, tends to swell and stiffen the ECM.
source: The latter, more hydrophilic than the first one, tends to swell and stiffen the ECM.
evidence: The claim is based on known properties of hyaluronan.

claim: The correlation between matrix mechanics and uncontrolled proliferation is more and more widely accepted.
source: Whether a corrupted matrix is a contributing cause or the consequence of the neoplasia remains an open question, but the correlation between matrix mechanics and uncontrolled proliferation is more and more widely accepted (Bissell et al., 2002; Lelièvre and Bissell, 2006; Broders-Bondon et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bissell et al., 2002, Lelièvre and Bissell, 2006, and Broders-Bondon et al., 2018.

claim: Global compressions have a strong impact on the aggregates growth and internal cell motility, while selective compressions of same magnitude have almost no effect.
source: By comparing results of selective osmotic compressions of CT26 mouse cells within multicellular aggregates and global aggregate compressions, we show that global compressions have a strong impact on the aggregates growth and internal cell motility, while selective compressions of same magnitude have almost no effect.
evidence: The claim is the main finding of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Both global and selective compressions alter the volume of individual cells in the same way over a short-timescale.
source: Both compressions alter the volume of individual cells in the same way over a shor-timescale, but, by draining the water out of the extracellular matrix, the global one imposes a residual compressive mechanical stress on the cells over a long-timescale, while the selective one does not.
evidence: The claim is a key finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: By draining the water out of the extracellular matrix, global compression imposes a residual compressive mechanical stress on the cells over a long-timescale, while selective compression does not.
source: Both compressions alter the volume of individual cells in the same way over a shor-timescale, but, by draining the water out of the extracellular matrix, the global one imposes a residual compressive mechanical stress on the cells over a long-timescale, while the selective one does not.
evidence: The claim is a key finding of the study, supported by experimental data and theoretical modeling.

claim: The extracellular matrix acts as a sensor that mechanically regulates cell proliferation and migration in a 3D environment.
source: We conclude that the extracellular matrix is as a sensor that mechanically regulates cell proliferation and migration in a 3D environment.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, inferred from all experimental results.

claim: Imposed deformations play an important role in morphogenesis and tissue homeostasis, both in normal and pathological conditions.
source: Imposed deformations play an important role in morphogenesis and tissue homeostasis, both in normal and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The ECM is a non-cellular component of tissues providing a scaffold for cellular adhesion and triggering numerous mechanotransduction pathways, involved in morphogenesis and homeostasis.
source: The ECM is a non-cellular component of tissues providing a scaffold for cellular adhesion and triggering numerous mechanotransduction pathways, involved in morphogenesis and homeostasis (Vogel, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vogel, 2018.

claim: Changing the mechanical properties of the ECM by re-implanting tissues or changing the stiffness of the adherent substrate is sufficient to reverse aging.
source: An increasing number of studies in vivo and in vitro shows that changing the mechanical properties of the ECM by re-implanting tissues or changing the stiffness of the adherent substrate is sufficient to reverse aging (Segel et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Segel et al., 2019.

claim: Changing the mechanical properties of the ECM can accelerate developmental processes.
source: An increasing number of studies in vivo and in vitro shows that changing the mechanical properties of the ECM by re-implanting tissues or changing the stiffness of the adherent substrate is sufficient to reverse aging (Segel et al., 2019), accelerate developmental processes (Barriga et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Barriga et al., 2018.

claim: Changing the mechanical properties of the ECM can modulate tumor malignancy.
source: An increasing number of studies in vivo and in vitro shows that changing the mechanical properties of the ECM by re-implanting tissues or changing the stiffness of the adherent substrate is sufficient to reverse aging (Segel et al., 2019), accelerate developmental processes (Barriga et al., 2018) or modulate tumor malignancy (Paszek et al., 2005; Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Paszek et al., 2005 and Tanner et al., 2012.

claim: The importance of the mechanical context in cancer has been highlighted by experiments altering the composition and stiffness of the ECM.
source: The importance of the mechanical context in cancer has been highlighted for a long time by experiments altering the composition and stiffness of the ECM (Levental et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Levental et al., 2009.

claim: Tumor growth is modulated by the mechanical compression caused by the tumor itself, as it expands in a confined environment.
source: It has also been shown that the tumor growth is modulated by the mechanical compression caused by the tumor itself, as it expands in a confined environment (Fernandez-Sanchez et al., 2010; Nia et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fernandez-Sanchez et al., 2010 and Nia et al., 2017.

claim: When multicellular aggregates are confined by soft gels, their growth is substantially reduced.
source: When multicellular aggregates are confined by soft gels (Helmlinger et al., 1997; Alessandri et al., 2013; Taubenberger et al., 2019) or submitted to a gentle osmotic compression (Montel et al., 2011; Dolega et al., 2017), their growth is substantially reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: When multicellular aggregates are submitted to a gentle osmotic compression, their growth is substantially reduced.
source: When multicellular aggregates are confined by soft gels (Helmlinger et al., 1997; Alessandri et al., 2013; Taubenberger et al., 2019) or submitted to a gentle osmotic compression (Montel et al., 2011; Dolega et al., 2017), their growth is substantially reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Montel et al., 2011 and Dolega et al., 2017.

claim: The cell cytoskeleton is involved in the response to compression and can trigger the growth impediment through a cell-cycle inhibition.
source: It has been demonstrated that the cell cytoskeleton is involved in the response to compression and can trigger the growth impediment through a cell-cycle inhibition (Taubenberger et al., 2019; Delarue et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Taubenberger et al., 2019 and Delarue et al., 2014.

claim: The cellular volume has been recently proposed to be a key parameter in the mechanosensitive pathway.
source: In addition, the cellular volume has been recently proposed to be a key parameter in the mechanosensitive pathway (Delarue et al., 2014; Han et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Delarue et al., 2014 and Han et al., 2020.

claim: An aggregate is a composite material made of cells, extracellular matrix and interstitial fluid.
source: First, an aggregate is a composite material made of cells, extracellular matrix and interstitial fluid.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about aggregate composition.

claim: CT26 cells are murine colon carcinoma cells.
source: Analogous experiments were performed using individual CT26 cells (murine colon carcinoma cells) and multicellular spheroids made with the same cell line.
evidence: This is a factual description of the cell line used.

claim: The division time of CT26 cells in 2D (Petri dish) with no pressure is 11.4 ± 0.5 hr.
source: Division time of CT26 cells in 2D (Petri dish), respectively with no pressure (11.4 ± 0.5 hr), with Πd=5 kPa/small dextran (11.0 ± 0.3 hr) and with Πd=5 kPa/big dextran (10.9 ± 0.4 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The division time of CT26 cells in 2D with Πd=5 kPa/small dextran is 11.0 ± 0.3 hr.
source: Division time of CT26 cells in 2D (Petri dish), respectively with no pressure (11.4 ± 0.5 hr), with Πd=5 kPa/small dextran (11.0 ± 0.3 hr) and with Πd=5 kPa/big dextran (10.9 ± 0.4 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The division time of CT26 cells in 2D with Πd=5 kPa/big dextran is 10.9 ± 0.4 hr.
source: Division time of CT26 cells in 2D (Petri dish), respectively with no pressure (11.4 ± 0.5 hr), with Πd=5 kPa/small dextran (11.0 ± 0.3 hr) and with Πd=5 kPa/big dextran (10.9 ± 0.4 hr).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4f.
